items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: There was a strollin' guitar [gi-tar] player, a guy who played guitar who was known in the town -- Black Hamp and...Black Nolan(?). Helluva guitar player.

ctx.x: Yeah. His brother was... There was brother who had a camp on the lake, dealt from it all his life. Dealt in fish and crabs for the restaurants in town. So while I had Creole food with my French people, my mother's people, and I had Country food with my grandmother and my father's people. They came out of New Iberia. I'll tell you how they got here later on.

But getting back to this music, there was music all around. Everywhere that guys could whistle. There was a strollin' guitar [gi-tar] player, a guy who played guitar who was known in the town -- Black Hamp and...Black Nolan(?). Helluva guitar player. That Folk guitar, that Leadbelly (?) that you play with your fingers.

ctx.x: And it was sitting on the wagon like this, two wheel wagon, you know, and sitting there and they had a regular contraption built that they sat inside of this. And the guy would hire it for a day, guaranteed to get a guy who owned it so much money. And he put it from bar to bar. A lot of guys made their living like this. And they had a big old bucket on it, so he would, at a corner he stopped to borrow it. The bartender would give him a pitcher of beer, a can of beer, a can of beer. He'd pass the hat around the…
did you recognize any of the guys later? Oh, later on I got to know them like, for instance, like

Black Nolan, Buckeye Wilford. What did they play? They played piano. All these were piano players? They played the blues, yeah, piano players. Black Nolan, Buckeye Wilford. Yeah, they were always welcome. Shine, regular hunky-tunk piano players. First time I heard what it's called now Boogie Woogie. The first time I heard that beat, my little uncle said, look at that guy playing them horses. He used to call it the horses in New Orleans.
